title: Slow Flight, Stall Aerodynamics & Recovery

required_knowledge_points.title: Slow Flight Aerodynamics — The Region of Reversed Command
required_knowledge_points.why: The DPE asks: 'What is the region of reversed command?' The answer reveals whether you understand the physics of flight at low speed. In normal flight, slow down = reduce power. In reversed command, slow down = ADD power. The relationship between pitch and power REVERSES — altitude is managed with the throttle, airspeed with pitch.
required_knowledge_points.knowledge: SLOW FLIGHT is conducted at an airspeed just above the stall warning threshold — the region of reversed command (back side of the power curve). DRAG PHYSICS: total drag = parasite drag + induced drag. Parasite drag increases with the square of airspeed. Induced drag increases with the inverse square of airspeed. Their intersection = L/D max (minimum total drag speed). Below L/D max, induced drag dominates. REVERSED COMMAND: below L/D max, if the pilot pitches up to slow further, induced drag spikes so rapidly that the current power setting cannot overcome total drag. The aircraft descends DESPITE the nose being pitched up. To maintain altitude at a slower speed, the pilot must ADD power. This is the reversal: altitude = throttle, airspeed = pitch. SPEED INSTABILITY: a uniquely dangerous property of reversed command. Any speed decrease causes drag to exceed thrust, which causes further speed decrease. This is a positive feedback loop — without pilot intervention, the aircraft decelerates into a stall. LEFT-TURNING TENDENCIES: amplified at high AOA with high power. P-Factor (asymmetric propeller thrust), torque, spiraling slipstream, and gyroscopic precession all yaw the nose LEFT. The pilot must apply continuous RIGHT RUDDER proportional to power setting and AOA. Failure to coordinate = skidding flight = foundation for a cross-control stall/spin.
required_knowledge_points.knowledge_formatted:
### The Drag Curve and Reversed Command
```
Drag
 │    \         /
 │     \  ↗   /        Parasite drag (increases with speed²)
 │      X             ← L/D max (minimum total drag)
 │     / \↙
 │    /     \          Induced drag (increases with 1/speed²)
 │   /       \
 └──────────────── Airspeed
     REVERSED   NORMAL
     COMMAND    COMMAND
```

### Control Reversal
| Parameter | Normal Command | Reversed Command |
|---|---|---|
| **Altitude** | Pitch controls | **Throttle** controls |
| **Airspeed** | Throttle controls | **Pitch** controls |

### Speed Instability (Positive Feedback Loop)
```
Speed decreases → drag increases → speed decreases more → stall
```
- In normal command: speed decrease → drag decrease → self-correcting
- In reversed command: speed decrease → drag INCREASE → **divergent**

### Left-Turning Tendencies in Slow Flight
| Force | Why Amplified | Mitigation |
|---|---|---|
| **P-Factor** | High AOA → descending blade bites more air | Right rudder |
| **Torque** | High power + slow speed | Right rudder |
| **Slipstream** | Wraps around fuselage → hits left side of vertical stabilizer | Right rudder |
| **Precession** | Pitch changes + spinning prop | Right rudder |

### ACS Tolerances
- Altitude: ±100 ft | Heading: ±10° | Airspeed: +10/-0 knots | Bank: ±10°

> ⚠️ **Checkride Trap:** 'What happens if you pitch up to maintain altitude in slow flight without adding power?' Induced drag spikes → airspeed decays → stall. You MUST add power.

required_knowledge_points.title: Stall Aerodynamics — Critical AOA, Boundary Layer, and Accelerated Stalls
required_knowledge_points.why: The DPE asks the single most important question in aerodynamics: 'Can an aircraft stall at cruise speed?' YES. A stall is ONLY a function of angle of attack. It can happen at any airspeed, any attitude, any power setting. The DPE also asks about accelerated stalls: 'What is the stall speed in a 60° bank?' It's Vs × √2 = 1.41 × Vs.
required_knowledge_points.knowledge: A stall occurs EXCLUSIVELY when the wing exceeds the critical angle of attack (AOA) — typically 15-20° for GA airfoils. At the critical AOA, the boundary layer cannot maintain laminar flow against the adverse pressure gradient on the upper wing surface. It separates, creating turbulent eddies. Lift drops precipitously and form drag spikes. THE ZERO-LIFT MYTH: a stalled wing does NOT produce zero lift. It produces insufficient lift to sustain level flight, but the wing still deflects air downward. If a stalled wing produced zero lift, the aircraft would be in 1G freefall. STALL AT ANY SPEED: the published stall speed (Vs) is valid ONLY for 1G unaccelerated flight. In a banked turn or abrupt pull-up, the wings must generate more lift to support the increased load factor. To generate more lift, AOA increases. The critical AOA is reached at a HIGHER airspeed. ACCELERATED STALL FORMULA: Vs(acc) = Vs × √n, where n = load factor (Gs). At 45° bank = 1.4G → Vs × 1.19. At 60° bank = 2.0G → Vs × 1.41. At 75° bank = 3.8G → Vs × 1.96. A Cessna 172 with Vs of 50 knots stalls at 70 knots in a 60° bank. CG EFFECT: forward CG increases stall speed because the horizontal stabilizer must generate more down-force, adding to the effective weight the wing must support. WING WASHOUT: the wing root has a higher angle of incidence than the wingtip — so the root stalls first. This preserves aileron effectiveness and generates aerodynamic buffet as the turbulent wake from the root hits the tail.
required_knowledge_points.knowledge_formatted:
### The Only Thing That Causes a Stall
**Exceeding the Critical Angle of Attack (AOA)**
- NOT low airspeed (airspeed is a proxy for AOA only at 1G)
- NOT nose-high attitude
- NOT power setting
- A stall CAN occur at **any airspeed, any attitude, any power setting**

### Accelerated Stall — Load Factor Table
| Bank Angle | Load Factor (G) | Stall Speed Multiplier | Example (Vs=50 kts) |
|---|---|---|---|
| **0°** (level) | 1.0 G | 1.00× | 50 kts |
| **30°** | 1.15 G | 1.07× | 54 kts |
| **45°** | 1.41 G | 1.19× | 59 kts |
| **60°** | 2.0 G | **1.41×** | **70 kts** |
| **75°** | 3.86 G | 1.96× | 98 kts |

### Wing Washout — Why Stalls Are Survivable
- Root incidence angle > tip incidence angle
- Root stalls **first** → turbulent wake hits tail → **buffet warning**
- Tips keep flying → **ailerons still work** through the stall break
- Without washout: entire wing stalls simultaneously → violent asymmetric departure

### Stall Recognition (Multisensory)
| Sense | Indicator |
|---|---|
| **Feel** | Sluggish controls, mushy yoke, buffet vibration |
| **Sound** | Stall horn (5-10 kts above stall), reduced wind noise |
| **Sight** | Abnormally high pitch attitude relative to horizon |

> ⚠️ **Checkride Trap:** 'Can an aircraft stall at 120 knots?' YES — if the pilot pulls enough G to increase the load factor and reach the critical AOA at 120 knots. Stall is about AOA, not airspeed.

required_knowledge_points.title: Power-Off Stall Scenarios and Risk Factors
required_knowledge_points.why: The DPE asks: 'What real-world scenario does the power-off stall simulate?' It simulates a stall during the approach and landing phase — specifically, the pilot who tries to stretch a glide to a runway by pulling back. Pulling back INCREASES drag, DECREASES glide distance, and stalls the wing. This scenario kills pilots at altitudes too low for recovery.
required_knowledge_points.knowledge: POWER-OFF STALLS simulate approach/landing phase hazards. THREE FATAL SCENARIOS: (1) STRETCHING THE GLIDE: pilot is short of the runway at idle power and pulls back to 'fly farther.' Aerodynamically, pulling back increases AOA → induced drag spikes → glide ratio WORSENS → airspeed decays → stall. The correct action: add power to extend the glide, or accept the undershoot and land short of the intended point. (2) WIND SHEAR: aircraft on final at 65 knots into a 20-knot headwind (groundspeed 45 knots). Aircraft descends below tree line, headwind drops to zero. Indicated airspeed INSTANTLY drops from 65 to 45 knots. If Vs is 50 knots, the aircraft is stalled. Mitigation: carry an additive speed factor in gusty conditions (half the gust factor). (3) HIGH FLARE: pilot rounds out too high above the runway and continues pulling back to hold the aircraft off the surface. Airspeed bleeds off → stall at 15 feet → hard landing or collapsed gear. Correct action: go around if the flare is too high. THE BASE-TO-FINAL TURN TRAP: the deadliest scenario. A tailwind on base increases groundspeed → pilot thinks they'll overshoot → applies inside rudder to tighten the turn instead of increasing bank → skidding turn → adds opposite aileron (cross-controlled) → pulls back because the nose is dropping → critical AOA exceeded while uncoordinated → SPIN. At 500 ft AGL, recovery is physically impossible. Prevention: go around if overshooting, or increase bank angle properly rather than using rudder.
required_knowledge_points.knowledge_formatted:
### Three Fatal Power-Off Stall Scenarios

#### 1. Stretching the Glide
```
Short of runway → pulls back → AOA increases → induced drag spikes
→ glide ratio WORSENS → sink rate INCREASES → stall at low altitude
→ NO recovery altitude available → FATAL
```
**Fix:** Add power or accept the undershoot. Never 'stretch' with pitch alone.

#### 2. Wind Shear on Final
```
Flying 65 kts into 20-kt headwind (groundspeed = 45 kts)
→ drops below tree line → headwind drops to 0
→ IAS instantly drops to 45 kts → Vs = 50 kts → STALLED
```
**Fix:** Carry additive speed (half the gust factor) in gusty conditions.

#### 3. The Base-to-Final Turn Trap
```
Tailwind on base → high groundspeed → think you'll overshoot
→ inside rudder to tighten turn (SKID)
→ opposite aileron to level wings (CROSS-CONTROL)
→ pull back because nose drops → EXCEED critical AOA
→ asymmetric stall → SPIN at 500 ft AGL → FATAL
```
**Fix:** Go around if overshooting. Never use rudder to tighten a turn.

### The Slip vs. Skid Life-or-Death Distinction
| Condition | If Stall Occurs... |
|---|---|
| **Slip** (rudder opposite turn) | Aircraft rolls OUT of turn → recoverable |
| **Skid** (rudder into turn) | Aircraft rolls INTO turn → **violent spin entry** |

> ⚠️ **Checkride Trap:** 'What kills pilots in the traffic pattern?' The base-to-final turn cross-control stall/spin. The DPE wants to hear: 'Go around if overshooting. Never use rudder to tighten a turn.'

required_knowledge_points.title: Stall Recovery — Reduce AOA, Manage Power, Avoid Secondary Stalls
required_knowledge_points.why: The DPE asks: 'Walk me through a stall recovery.' There is ONLY one cure for a stall: reduce the angle of attack. Not power. Not ailerons. REDUCE AOA — relax back pressure or push forward. Power helps minimize altitude loss but cannot un-stall a wing. And the most dangerous moment is the pull-out — pull too hard and you trigger a secondary stall.
required_knowledge_points.knowledge: STALL RECOVERY — THE PRIME DIRECTIVE: reduce the angle of attack below the critical AOA. This is the ONLY aerodynamic cure. No amount of power, rudder, or aileron can un-stall a wing while the AOA remains above critical. STEP 1 — REDUCE AOA: relax back pressure or smoothly push the elevator forward. The pitch attitude drops relative to the flight path. The AOA decreases. When it drops below the critical threshold (~15-20°), the boundary layer reattaches, lift is restored. STEP 2 — APPLY POWER: maximum allowable power to minimize altitude loss. Power accelerates the aircraft, increasing dynamic pressure over the wings and generating more lift at lower AOAs. In propeller aircraft, the slipstream re-energizes the boundary layer over the wing root and empennage. STEP 3 — LEVEL THE WINGS: use coordinated flight inputs to return to wings-level. CRITICAL HAZARDS: SECONDARY STALL — after the initial stall breaks, the aircraft is nose-down and accelerating toward the ground. The pilot must pull back to level off. If the pull is TOO AGGRESSIVE, the AOA exceeds the critical threshold again → secondary stall. Secondary stalls are often more violent and result in greater altitude loss. AILERON DISCIPLINE — if a wing drops during the stall, do NOT use ailerons to pick it up. Deflecting the aileron down on the stalled wing INCREASES its AOA, deepening the stall on that wing and creating the asymmetric forces that produce a spin. Use RUDDER to control roll until the stall is broken. THE 'POWER-OUT' FALLACY — attempting to recover with full power ALONE, without releasing back pressure. Most GA aircraft do not have enough thrust-to-weight ratio to 'power out' of a fully stalled wing.
required_knowledge_points.knowledge_formatted:
### Stall Recovery Sequence
```
1. REDUCE AOA → relax back pressure or push forward
   (The ONLY aerodynamic cure — nothing else works first)
2. APPLY POWER → max allowable to minimize altitude loss
   (Power helps but CANNOT un-stall the wing alone)
3. LEVEL WINGS → coordinated flight inputs
4. PULL OUT → smooth, gentle back pressure to level flight
   (Too aggressive = secondary stall)
```

### Three Fatal Recovery Errors
| Error | Why It Kills | Correct Action |
|---|---|---|
| **Using ailerons on wing drop** | Increases AOA on stalled wing → spin entry | Use **rudder** to control roll |
| **Aggressive pull-out** | Exceeds critical AOA again → secondary stall | **Smooth**, gentle back pressure |
| **Power only, no AOA reduction** | Wing stays stalled despite full power | Relax back pressure **FIRST** |

### The Power-Out Fallacy
- Most GA aircraft: thrust-to-weight ≈ 0.1
- Cannot overcome drag of a fully stalled wing with power alone
- Power helps AFTER AOA is reduced — never INSTEAD of it

### Secondary Stall
- Occurs during pull-out from initial stall recovery
- Pilot pulls too hard → AOA exceeds critical again
- Often more violent than the initial stall
- Can occur at HIGHER airspeed due to G-loading (accelerated stall)

> ⚠️ **Checkride Trap:** 'What is the FIRST thing you do in a stall?' REDUCE THE ANGLE OF ATTACK. Not add power. Not level the wings. Reduce AOA.

lesson_overview:
## Slow Flight, Stall Aerodynamics, and Recovery — The Physics of Loss of Control

This lesson covers the aerodynamics of slow flight and stalls — the single most important body of knowledge for preventing Loss of Control In-Flight (LOC-I), the leading cause of fatal accidents in general aviation.

**Slow flight exists in the region of reversed command, where the normal relationship between pitch and power is inverted.** Below L/D max speed, induced drag dominates total drag. Slowing further requires MORE power, not less, because the exponential rise in induced drag demands additional thrust to maintain altitude. This reversal creates a dangerous property: speed instability. Any unintended speed loss increases drag, which causes further speed loss — a positive feedback loop that decelerates the aircraft toward the stall unless the pilot actively intervenes. Operating in this regime also amplifies every left-turning tendency: P-factor, torque, spiraling slipstream, and gyroscopic precession all yaw the nose left, demanding continuous right rudder that varies with power and angle of attack.

**A stall is exclusively a function of exceeding the critical angle of attack — not low airspeed, not a specific attitude, not a particular power setting.** The published stall speed in the POH applies only to unaccelerated 1G flight. In a 60-degree banked turn, the load factor doubles to 2G, and the stall speed increases by 41%. An aircraft that normally stalls at 50 knots will stall at 70 knots in that bank angle. This is the accelerated stall — a primary killer during low-altitude maneuvering where the pilot may feel 'safe' because the airspeed indicator reads well above the published stall speed. The wing itself is engineered with washout — a geometric twist that ensures the root stalls before the tips, providing buffet warning through the tail and preserving aileron effectiveness through the stall break.

**Power-off stalls simulate the approach and landing phase, where three scenarios kill pilots.** The 'stretching the glide' trap occurs when a pilot, short of the runway, pulls back to fly farther — but pulling back increases AOA and induced drag, WORSENING the glide ratio. Wind shear on final can instantly drop indicated airspeed below the stall speed when a headwind disappears behind terrain. And the base-to-final turn trap — the deadliest scenario in general aviation — occurs when a pilot uses inside rudder to tighten a turn (creating a skid), adds opposite aileron (cross-controlling), and pulls back (exceeding the critical AOA). The resulting spin at 500 feet AGL is unrecoverable.

**Stall recovery has one prime directive: reduce the angle of attack.** This is the only aerodynamic cure. Power helps minimize altitude loss but cannot un-stall a wing while the AOA remains above critical. The recovery sequence is: reduce AOA, apply power, level wings, and smoothly pull out. The pull-out phase is the most dangerous — aggressive back pressure triggers a secondary stall that is often more violent than the initial break. And a dropped wing must be controlled with RUDDER, not ailerons — deflecting an aileron down on a stalled wing increases its local AOA, deepening the stall and creating the asymmetric forces that drive an autorotative spin.
